title: Hash functions and buckets
summary: Turn any key into an array index, and deal with two keys that land in the same place.

steps.title: From key to index
body: Arrays are fast because `a[i]` jumps straight to slot `i`. A **hash table** gets the same speed for keys that are not numbers, like `"cat"`, by turning the key into a number first.
A **hash function** mixes the key into an integer. Then `hash % buckets` picks one of the table's slots, called **buckets**.
Watch the classic string hash below: for each character, multiply the running hash by 31 and add the character's code (`'c'` is 99, `'a'` is 97, `'t'` is 116).

steps.prompt: Same function, a shorter key. `'h'` is 104 and `'i'` is 105. What does it print?
Which property must **every** hash function have?
options: Equal keys always give the same hash
Different keys always give different hashes
The hash is always smaller than the number of buckets
The hash is a prime number
steps.explain: If `"cat"` hashed differently on the second lookup you would search the wrong bucket. Different keys *may* share a hash: there are far more possible strings than integers.

steps.title: Collisions and chaining
body: Two different keys can land in the same bucket: a **collision**. The common fix is **chaining**: each bucket holds a small list of everything that landed there.
Below, integer keys use `key % 4` as the bucket. `3`, `7` and `11` all land in bucket 3, so its list grows to three items. A lookup in bucket 3 now has to check up to three keys.
With a good hash spreading keys evenly, lists stay short and lookups are **O(1) on average**. If every key collided, one bucket would hold them all and lookups would decay to **O(n)**.

code: for (var b = 0; b < buckets.Length; b++) buckets[b] = new List<int>();

steps.prompt: Five buckets this time. What does it print?
code: for (var b = 0; b < buckets.Length; b++) buckets[b] = new List<int>();
steps.explain: 10 and 15 go to bucket 0; 3, 8 and 23 all go to bucket 3. A poor spread: keys that share a pattern pile up together.

steps.prompt: With 8 buckets and `key % 8`, which bucket does each key land in?
A table's **load factor** is items ÷ buckets. Why do hash tables grow (and redistribute their keys) when it passes about 0.75?
options: More items per bucket means longer chains and slower lookups
The hash function stops working above 0.75
Buckets can hold at most 0.75 items
steps.explain: Doubling the buckets halves the average chain length. Like `List<T>` doubling, the occasional rebuild is amortised O(1).

steps.title: Your own hash
prompt: - `int Hash(string s)`: start at 0; for each character, `hash = hash * 31 + c`. Let it overflow (C# wraps around by default). `Hash("cat")` is `98262`.
- `int BucketOf(string s, int buckets)`: the bucket for `s`, always between `0` and `buckets - 1`.
Careful: once the hash overflows it can be **negative**, and `%` of a negative number is negative in C#. `-7 % 4` is `-3`. Fix it up so the bucket is never negative.
solution: foreach (var c in s) hash = unchecked(hash * 31 + c);
template: Dojo.Eq("a long key wraps around to a negative hash", -1396355227, Hash("banana"));
var dojoWords = new[] { "apple", "banana", "cherry", "a much longer key than the others", "zzzzzzzzzzzz", "Q" };
Dojo.Check("every bucket is between 0 and 6", dojoWords.All(w => BucketOf(w, 7) is >= 0 and < 7), "a bucket was out of range");
hints: `foreach (var c in s) hash = hash * 31 + c;` A `char` adds as its number.
In `BucketOf`, if `b` is negative add `buckets` to it.
